verified.label: Verified
verified.note: Read directly from an artifact — a constant in a disassembly, a literal in a script, a symbol in a table, a part number in a service manual. Not dependent on interpretation.

inferred.label: Inferred
inferred.note: A reading of verified evidence that is well supported but not directly stated. The reasoning is given, and so are the competing readings.

unknown.label: Unknown
unknown.note: The artifacts show it exists, but its content, layout or semantics have not been determined.

public.label: Public
public.note: Taken from a datasheet, standard, service manual or the manufacturer's own published documentation. No analysis was needed.

statuses.label: Documented
statuses.note: A written teardown exists and its claims carry evidence citations.

statuses.label: Partial
statuses.note: Substantial findings recorded, but whole subsystems remain unexamined.

statuses.label: Active
statuses.note: Work in progress; the hardware inventory is not yet confirmed against a bench.

statuses.label: Reference design
statuses.note: Not a teardown — our own open design, included as the contrast case the teardowns keep pointing at.

statuses.label: Candidate
statuses.note: Named in existing work only as a comparison point. No analysis has been performed.

platforms.summary: A nine-processor console whose mixing DSPs have no instruction memory at all — the audio path is fixed-function silicon configured through a register file.
platforms.headline: The five YSS919C "DSP7" mixing chips expose a 512-word register file and no program port. This was proven not just from the pin tables but from absence: every region of the 64 MB flash is accounted for and there is no DSP7 program image anywhere in it.
platforms.method: Static analysis of the V5.91 USB firmware update package, cross-referenced against the published service manual's LSI pin descriptions. No console was involved and no hardware was inspected.
artifacts: `MQLP5_91.PGM` — 27.5 MB main-CPU image (console application + GUI resource pack)
`QL-MD103.BIN` — 110 KB channel-name display sub-MCU image
`FWUpdate_QL1_v4020401_sw310.dnt` — 4.7 MB Audinate Brooklyn II package
Service manual, LSI PIN DESCRIPTION section
`QL Editor.app` — Premium Rack plugins shipped as unstripped x86_64 dylibs

software.label: Operating system
software.value: Renesas HI7000/4-family µITRON 4.0 kernel. No Linux anywhere

software.label: Image load base
software.value: 0x8803BF80 — P1 space, so physical 0x0803BF80 = SDRAM + 0x3BF80. The image is placed in RAM by a bootloader not present in the .PGM

software.label: Code volume
software.value: ≈7 MB of SH-4A little-endian machine code; the remainder is GUI resources

software.label: Task model
software.value: ~130 named µITRON objects across kernel, panel bus, display, mix engine, Premium Rack, MIDI, Dante, network, L2 switch and remote control

software.label: Debug facilities
software.value: Live serial debug monitor (task/sema/flag/mbox/mpl/mbf commands) plus Hitachi DT10 trace instrumentation still present in shipping firmware

software.label: Plugin ABI
software.value: Premium Rack plugins export `createPerseusPlugin_203` — the identical symbol appears in the console firmware (`-sh4a-per`) and in the macOS editor's dylibs (`-mac-per`)

software.label: Console plugin linkage
software.value: Statically linked into the main firmware image, not shipped as separate files

security.label: Image signing
security.value: None found

security.label: Encryption
security.value: None — the package is plainly structured and its components are directly readable

programmable.note: The cheapest route to putting custom DSP in the audio path with no console modification at all. Host aperture 0xBA002000 + (slot << 11), 16-bit port on A10..A1.
The audio crossbar between Dante, every DSP7, the SHARC, the DSP6 bank and both slots. JTAG header present, and it is configurable from the CPU. Highest leverage, least investigated.

The Premium Rack engine. A documented part, SPI-slave boot, JTAG header already fitted. Eight stereo slots means up to 16 mono inserts, patchable from the console's own UI. The one place third-party code could plausibly run.

platforms.verdict: The mixing engine is closed by construction rather than by policy — there is no software on it to replace. The programmable surface is real but sits alongside the mix engine, not inside it.
openQuestions: The patch FPGA's configuration path from the CPU has not been traced.
The DSP7 register-file semantics are undocumented; only the bus interface is known.
No claim here has been checked against a physical QL console.
traps: The image load base is 0x8803BF80, not 0x88000000. The wrong value looks entirely plausible and silently yields almost no valid cross-references.
Never attribute an MMIO constant from string-pool proximity. Doing so produced a claim that 0xBA002000 was the DSP7 window when it is the slot aperture — published, then retracted.

platforms.summary: Nine years newer than the QL and sharing almost nothing with it but the parameter framework — including, crucially, the same DSP philosophy.
platforms.headline: The update package is a named-component archive (`#YAMAHA MBDFArchive`) carrying a full Linux rootfs, and the installer is a plain bash script with no checksum ceremony and no signature. Unlike the QL, the DSP arrives as a loadable 3.8 MB image.
platforms.method: Static analysis of the V3.00 firmware package (167 MB) and the macOS DM3 Editor. Nothing has been tested on hardware.
artifacts: `DM3_firmware_V3.00.bin` — 167 MB, eleven named components
`DM3 Editor.app` (macOS)

hardware.label: Application processor
hardware.value: Runs a Linux userland — component 1 is an 88 MB rootfs tarball

hardware.label: FPGA
hardware.value: Present — component 3, `fab_V110.bin`, 539 KB inflated

hardware.label: DSP
hardware.value: Present as a loadable image — component 4, `DSP_V121.bin`, 3.80 MB inflated

hardware.label: Panel MCU
hardware.value: Component 2, `DM3PN_V100.bin`, 246 KB inflated

hardware.label: Audio networking
hardware.value: Audinate Brooklyn 3 plus a Broadway module — components 5 and 6

software.label: Container format
software.value: `#YAMAHA MBDFArchive` — magic, model, version and a 16-byte digest, then `#FIRMWARE` records of five BE u32 fields, three NUL-terminated strings (path / description / version) and a zlib payload, terminated by `#END`

software.label: Main application
software.value: `app_console.tgz`, 64.8 MB inflated, V3.00

software.label: Installer
software.value: A bash script. Untars to /tmp/update, walks /yamaha/firmware.new/, compares each component's version file against the installed one and copies only what changed, running a per-component `<name>.sh` hook if present

software.label: Bootloader
software.value: Shipped as an updatable component — `app_bootloader.tgz`, V1.03

security.label: Image signing
security.value: None — the installer performs no signature check

security.label: Integrity
security.value: A 16-byte digest in the archive header; no checksum ceremony in the install path

security.label: Encryption
security.value: None — every component is zlib, and unpacks with a 60-line script

programmable.note: A conventional userland behind an unsigned, script-driven installer is a materially different proposition from the QL's µITRON image.
Unlike the QL's fixed-function DSP7s, the DM3 loads a 3.8 MB DSP image at update time. What accepts it has not been identified.

platforms.verdict: The interesting contrast with the QL is not the CPU or the OS — it is that the DSP is loadable here. That single fact changes what a modification would even mean on this platform.
openQuestions: Which silicon consumes `DSP_V121.bin`, and in what format.
The FPGA part has not been identified.
No board has been inspected and no claim has been checked on hardware.

platforms.summary: A 55 MB firmware image that contains none of the mixer. The entire audio path lives in FPGA fabric behind an undocumented AXI register map.
platforms.headline: The update package is 55 MB of ARM image and 2.5 MB of bitstream — and the 2.5 MB is the mixer. Most of the 55 MB is uncompressed UI artwork.
platforms.method: Static analysis of a single vendor firmware update file. No hardware was inspected. The firmware image was not retained, so the analysis currently cannot be re-derived without obtaining it again.
artifacts: `SQ-5UPG_1_6_3r6268.bin` — three records, no compression, no encryption

hardware.label: SoC
hardware.value: Xilinx Zynq-7000 XC7Z020 — proven from the bitstream's IDCODE configuration packet (30018001 → 03727093), not inferred

hardware.label: Corroboration
hardware.value: Linked Xilinx PS drivers: xemacps, xscugic, xdevcfg, xqspips, xiicps, xttcps, xuartps, plus lwIP 2.0.3 (xilinx_modified)

hardware.label: FPGA count
hardware.value: One. xdevcfg with PCAP_FPGA_DONE_FAIL shows the bitstream loading into this same chip's PL over the PCAP bridge — there is no second FPGA

hardware.label: DRAM
hardware.value: ≥1 GB — inferred from CPU1's 0x20100000 load address (513 MB in) against the Zynq-7000 PS ceiling of 1 GB. No memory-controller config was decoded

hardware.label: Boot flash
hardware.value: Dual-parallel QSPI NOR, ~64 MB (`InitQspi2Dual`). Dual-parallel means two devices striped — a naive single-chip dump gets every other byte

hardware.label: Surface MCU
hardware.value: A fader/surface MCU flashed over SPI from the ARM (`Expected Fader Version %u.%u, updating...`)

hardware.label: FX board
hardware.value: Separate board with its own DSPs and SDRAM (`FX board ID 0x%02X not recognised`, `FX[0] failed SDRAM test`)

software.label: Operating system
software.value: None. Zero FreeRTOS, ThreadX or Linux strings — a bare-metal Xilinx standalone BSP with a custom message-block system and a custom GUI

software.label: Core model
software.value: AMP across both Cortex-A9s, not SMP. `CPU0: sending Start Msg to CPU1`

software.label: CPU0
software.value: `sQu_Host` at 0x00100000 — mixer control, GUI, protocols

software.label: CPU1
software.value: `sQu_USB` at 0x20100000 — SQ-Drive: USB host, FAT, WAV. Directory layout /AHSQ/USBRec, /AHSQ/Scenes, /AHSQ/Shows appears verbatim

software.label: Container header
software.value: 0x70 (112) bytes, computed as next_offset − this_offset − payload_len and confirmed independently at both gaps. It is not read from any field

software.label: Payload format
software.value: Despite `.elf` names the payloads are raw ARM32 images, each with a 16-byte preamble; byte 16 onward is the ARM exception vector table

software.label: Code fraction
software.value: Only ~10–16 MB of the 55 MB host image is code. From 16 MB on it compresses to 9–27%, i.e. uncompressed artwork and fonts

security.label: Image signing
security.value: None. No RSA, SHA or AES strings anywhere in either image

security.label: Update validation
security.value: CRC only, and the variant was not identified — `Error in firmware header`, `VerifyFlash Expected CRC to be 0x%lx, but calculated 0x%lx`

security.label: Bitstream encryption
security.value: Not encrypted. The CTL0 write is 0x00001501 with the DEC bit (bit 6) clear and no key-load sequence, so the bitstream is analysable

security.label: Recovery
security.value: A/B image banks with Zynq multiboot. The update overwrites the inactive bank; the first-stage bootloader is not in the update file and is not protected by the A/B scheme

security.label: Entitlement
security.value: An entitlement mechanism exists and was identified. Analysis stopped there — see the methodology page

programmable.note: The SLink slot takes gigaACE, Dante and Waves cards, and Allen & Heath publish the SQ MIDI/TCP control protocol. Almost anything that motivated looking at the firmware in the first place is better served here, and none of it needs reverse engineering.

programmable.item: The AXI register map — the one thing genuinely worth reversing
programmable.note: Map the PS↔PL interface and the black box becomes documented hardware: you could drive the stock mixing engine from your own software, which is a far better position than replacing either half. It is also reachable non-destructively, with the stock bitstream loaded and nothing written to flash.

Unencrypted, and Project X-Ray covers Artix-7 and Zynq-7 fabric, so it is analysable in principle. In practice it is a very large project and it is downstream of understanding the register map anyway. Not step one.
Entirely feasible and almost pointless on its own — it gets you Linux wired to a black box you cannot command. Worth doing only as a means of probing the AXI map.

platforms.verdict: A poor rehosting target, but not for the usual reasons. There is no secure boot and no signing — yet none of the mixer is in the software you would replace. If it were ever pursued, the correct first move is JTAG, not the USB update path: dump the 64 MB QSPI intact before writing anything.
openQuestions: The PL's AXI register map is entirely undocumented — this is the whole audio path, and it is the single most important missing piece.
The FX board's DSPs are a genuine gap: not the vendor, not the architecture, not how code reaches them. The `FX[0]` indexing implies more than one.
The first-stage bootloader is not in the update file and has never been seen. The A/B banks protect the application images, not it.
The debug UART is near-certainly populated (xuartps is linked and printf diagnostics are everywhere) but has never been located on a board.
traps: A parser assuming a 0x24 or 0x40 container header parses record 0 plausibly and then lands mid-payload in 55 MB of ARM code and artwork.
The correct load mapping for the host image is VA = file offset + 0x103DD0, pinned empirically from the GUI string-pointer table — not the 0x100000 the container header implies.
GUI strings are reached through a master string-pointer table indexed by string ID, so they have no direct LDR-literal cross-reference. Only BSP and system strings are loaded directly.

platforms.summary: The one console examined whose control plane is wide open: a full Linux computer speaking documented Thrift and Protobuf. The mixer still lives in FPGA fabric — but the bitstreams ship in the clear and the exact parts are known.
platforms.headline: Three stacked computers: a Jetson TK1 runs the GUI and the control protocols, an ARM920T card runs the mixer, and the mixing itself is an unencrypted Spartan-6 bitstream that ships inside the update.
platforms.method: Static analysis of the public 2.4.0 firmware bundle — a signed APT repository plus Yocto board images. No hardware was inspected. The bundle was retained, so every claim here re-derives from it. Two protocol schemas were recovered whole: the Thrift RPC from shipped generated Python, the Protobuf bus from descriptors embedded in a shared library.
artifacts: `hd96_2.4.0+sumo.329.tar` — VERSION/WHATSNEW/`CHECKSUMS`(.asc), `repo.tar` (APT repo, 108 debs), `mghd271-tk1-*.tar.gz` (Yocto images)
`libPufferfishCore.so` — embeds all 13 control-bus `FileDescriptorProto`s
`as88_hmac.bin` / `as88_smac.bin` — the mix-engine FPGA bitstreams, shipped inside `mkt-as88`

hardware.label: Host SoC
hardware.value: NVIDIA Tegra124 (Jetson TK1), quad Cortex-A15 — from the device tree `compatible = "nvidia,jetson-tk1","nvidia,tegra124"` and the `armhf` package architecture

hardware.label: Host DRAM
hardware.value: 2 GB — the DT memory node is `reg = <0x80000000 0x80000000>`. A 4 GB boot-config (`bct_hyinx_4gb`) also ships, so a 4 GB surface variant exists

hardware.label: Mix-engine card (AS88)
hardware.value: A separate board hosting the mixer: an ARM920T running a Buildroot 2013.08 / uClibc Linux under the RedBoot bootloader, from 32 MB of NOR flash mapped at `0x60000000`. Build path `KES-BR14-ARM920T`, RedBoot FIS table intact

hardware.label: Mixing FPGA (HMAC)
hardware.value: Xilinx Spartan-6 XC6SLX100 — proven from the bitstream's own IDCODE register write (`0x04011093`) in `as88_hmac.bin`, not inferred

hardware.label: AES50 SuperMAC FPGA (SMAC)
hardware.value: Xilinx Spartan-6 XC6SLX150 — IDCODE `0x0401D093` in `as88_smac.bin`. This is the Klark Teknik SuperMAC/HyperMAC AES50 fabric

hardware.label: Host-side FPGAs
hardware.value: Routing and IO on the TK1 side: `mkt-fpga-{io,io2,ve,ctrl,hd272-ctrl,hd272-audio}` plus expansion-card ASRC/AES50 images, flashed by `mkt-fpga`

hardware.label: FX DSPs
hardware.value: An Analog-Devices-SHARC-family DSP subsystem reached through `/dev/dayak`; 63 effects ship as loadable `*_MultiApp` DSP images. Part not pinned — inferred from `ADSP-` strings and the loader format

hardware.label: Ethernet switch
hardware.value: Marvell `mv88e6096` managed switch, configured over memory-mapped IO-FPGA access (`mkt-hd271-switch-config`)

hardware.label: Expansion / STM32
hardware.value: An STM32 “HD271C” expansion-card handler (`mkt-hermes`) drives AES50 option cards and DP48 stageboxes; IO boxes are controlled in-band over the AES50 port (`HardwareControlOverAesPort`)

software.label: Host OS
software.value: Full embedded Linux — Yocto “sumo”, `ID=hd271dist` 2.20.1, kernel 3.10.40, u-boot 2014.10. Not bare metal

software.label: Application layer
software.value: A signed APT repository of 108 packages (57 first-party `mkt-*`) layered on the Yocto rootfs; `mkt-heritage` is the top-level that pulls in the whole console

software.label: GUI
software.value: `squig` — a CEF/Chromium-backed application (cef-runtime 3770), run as `offlinesquig … --allowRemoteClients true`

software.label: Control bus
software.value: `pufferfish` — Protobuf over ZMQ/TCP on port 9990, advertised over mDNS as “HD96Control”. The complete proto3 schema (13 files, namespace `serialisation`) was recovered from embedded descriptors

software.label: Parameter model
software.value: A string-key + category addressed tree: `ParameterRequest{subscribe|unsubscribe; identifier{category|key}}` → `ParameterEvent{Parameter{key,value,categories}}`, values a 10-arm `ConsoleValue` union. Show control is a 41-verb `AutomationEvent` enum (recall / store / loadShow / fireEvent / import·exportShow)

software.label: Test RPC
software.value: `razorbill` — Apache Thrift on port 9094, three privilege tiers up to a 60-method development interface (SetParameterValue, Screenshot, InstallPackage, Reboot, user-DB inject/wipe). The IDL was read back from shipped generated Python

software.label: Surface variants
software.value: HD96-16, HD96-24 and HD96 Air, six surface bays and dual mix engines (HMAC1/HMAC2) — leaked verbatim by the `DebugEvent` enum (`surfaceConfigHd96_16_revA`, `_24_revD`, `_Air_revA`)

security.label: Package trust
security.value: The update is a GPG-signed APT repo (Origin “Music Group Research UK”) with a SHA-256 `CHECKSUMS` manifest and a detached PGP signature over it. Package-level integrity, not silicon secure boot

security.label: Mixing bitstream encryption
security.value: None. Both Spartan-6 bitstreams ship unencrypted — the AA·99·55·66 sync word is in the clear and there is no key-load sequence. They are byte-bit-reversed for flash storage, nothing more

security.label: Host secure boot
security.value: No evidence of fused Tegra secure boot. u-boot carries the Tegra `bootsecure`/BCT infrastructure, but nothing indicates the fuses are burned on shipping hardware

security.label: Control-plane auth
security.value: None observed. `razorbill` Thrift is a plain `TBinaryProtocol` server with no authentication; `squig` runs with --allowRemoteClients true. Whether 9990/9094 bind off-box on a shipping desk is unconfirmed

security.label: Entitlement
security.value: A device-uniqueness / licensing mechanism exists (`mkt-uniqueness`, the mCloud proxy). Its content was not analysed — see the methodology page

programmable.note: `pufferfish` (Protobuf, :9990) is a live parameter/metering bus and `razorbill` (Thrift, :9094) a full control RPC. Both schemas are recovered. This is a console you can speak to today, and it is where the value is.
Unencrypted and identified (XC6SLX100 / XC6SLX150), so analysable with Project X-Ray. But replacing it means writing a mix engine against an unpublished pinout and an ARM920T host interface.
Trivially Linux-friendly — but replacing the TK1 software leaves you wired to the same engine cards, which is the part that actually mixes. It buys nothing, exactly as on the SQ-5.

platforms.verdict: The most open console examined. The mixer still lives in FPGA fabric, as on the SQ-5 — but here the bitstreams ship in the clear, the exact Spartan-6 parts are known from their IDCODEs, and, unlike the SQ, the entire control plane is documented RPC you can speak now. The value is interop, and it is unusually reachable; rehosting remains pointless for the same reason it was on the SQ.
openQuestions: Do ports 9990 and 9094 bind off-box on a shipping desk, and is the Protobuf bus authenticated? The mDNS advert and --allowRemoteClients true suggest reachable, but this was never tested on hardware.
The parameter key/category namespace — the actual channel/bus/FX addressing — is the last missing piece for real show control, and needs a live console to enumerate.
The register/AXI interface between the ARM920T host and the HMAC Spartan-6 is undocumented — the same black box the SQ-5 has, one layer down.
The exact SHARC part and the _MultiApp DSP loader format are unexamined.
traps: Two unrelated “HMAC”: the Midas mix-engine path, and hmac-md5/hmac-sha crypto strings in the AS88 rootfs. They are not related.
The FPGA bitstreams are byte-bit-reversed for flash, so a naive search for the AA·99·55·66 sync word fails until each byte is reversed.

The embedded Protobuf descriptors cannot be carved by binary-searching the length — descriptor validity is not monotonic. A field-by-field wire-format walk is required to find each descriptor's exact end.

platforms.summary: The only platform here being studied to build on rather than to understand — and the only one where the container format was analysed, found opaque, and then declared off the critical path.
platforms.headline: The `.wingfw` container is opaque but structured, and specifically not a block cipher: the index of coincidence is flat across every stride from 1 to 1024, so there is no repeating key — and all 171 constant runs of ≥64 bytes are 0xFF with not one 0x00 run. No block cipher leaves those.
platforms.method: Static analysis of a vendor firmware image, plus published datasheets and standards. No hardware has been acquired, so every hardware row is provisional and marked accordingly. A written clean-room policy governs the project.
artifacts: A `.wingfw` release image, version 3.1.1 (fullsize variant — nothing learned from it may be assumed to hold for Compact)
NXP i.MX 6 datasheet and reference manual
Analog Devices and Efinix product documentation

hardware.label: SoC
hardware.value: NXP i.MX 6 series, ARM Cortex-A9, MAPBGA 624

hardware.label: Core count
hardware.value: 1 (Solo-class) — to be confirmed by reading SCU config on hardware

hardware.label: DRAM
hardware.value: 1 GB at architectural base 0x10000000. Size unconfirmed — read the part markings

hardware.label: Boot flash
hardware.value: SPI-NOR, ~8 MB, s25fl064k-class. Unconfirmed

hardware.label: DSP
hardware.value: 4 × Analog Devices ADSP-21489 SHARC — where the mixing actually happens

hardware.label: FPGA
hardware.value: Efinix Trion T55 or T85 — the I/O fabric, not the mixer. Converter TDM, clock tree, AES50, StageConnect, AES/EBU and DSP links

hardware.label: FPGA config
hardware.value: SPI slave from the i.MX 6

hardware.label: Network switch
hardware.value: Marvell 88E6085 behind the i.MX 6 FEC, RMII 100 Mbit fixed-link. Unconfirmed

hardware.label: AES50
hardware.value: etherCON, 100BASE-TX physical layer. Whether a discrete PHY sits behind each port is unknown and decides whether those ports could ever carry anything else

hardware.label: Clock tree
hardware.value: Steerable (VCXO/DCO) or fixed crystals — unknown. This single question decides whether AES67 is possible on this hardware at all

hardware.label: StageConnect
hardware.value: USB-C physical layer, 32 channels

hardware.label: Panel
hardware.value: LVDS 1280×800, USB HID touch, motorised faders, per-strip colour scribble LCDs. Panel timings deliberately not recorded — they belong to the panel's datasheet

software.label: Boot path
software.value: The i.MX 6 has a documented, public boot ROM with a USB serial-download path. This is the fact that makes the whole project viable

software.label: Container
software.value: `.wingfw`, 38,873,600 bytes for the 3.1.1 fullsize release — no header and no magic. Entropy 7.37 bits/byte overall, first 2 MB flat at 8.00, remainder 6.1–7.5

software.label: Container — byte statistics
software.value: Histogram strongly skewed low: 0x00 at 5.6%, then 0x02, 0x01, 0x08 and 0x0f each around 2.6–3.0% against a uniform 0.39%. That rules out AES over the bulk. Index of coincidence flat across every stride 1–1024, so no repeating XOR key. No ECB structure

software.label: Container — negative sweeps
software.value: No squashfs, ELF, gzip, xz, zstd, UBI, JFFS2, cramfs, DTB, uImage, zImage or i.MX IVT magic — none plain, and none under 256 XOR constants, 256 additive constants, nibble swap, bit reversal or positional XOR. A brute-force deflate/zlib/LZMA sweep over the first 8 MB returned zero hits

software.label: Container verdict
software.value: Opaque but structured, and not a block cipher. Decoding it is never required in order to write a replacement OS

software.label: DSP toolchain
software.value: ADI CrossCore — proprietary, licensed

software.label: FPGA toolchain
software.value: Efinix Efinity — free, but proprietary

security.label: Secure boot
security.value: Unknown, and it is the project's kill criterion. If the i.MX 6 HAB fuses are burned closed, the platform is not open and the work stops

security.label: Container
security.value: Obfuscated by a mechanism not yet identified. Analysed, unsolved, and off the critical path

programmable.item: The i.MX 6 boot ROM, over USB OTG
programmable.note: Publicly documented in the NXP reference manual, requires no cooperation from the stock software, and is also the recovery path — which is why it is the one route worth proving before anything else is attempted. Conditional on the HAB fuses.

programmable.item: USB audio on the host port
programmable.note: A measurement path that sidesteps the converter, TDM and DSP problem entirely, so it can never be blocked by the hard part. Deliberately staged first for exactly that reason.

programmable.item: The four SHARCs and the Trion fabric
programmable.note: Documented parts. Bringing them up from nothing, alongside AES50, is the mountain — and the whole open-ended schedule risk lives here.
Ranked last on purpose. It needs the container solved, and the container is explicitly not on the critical path: writing a replacement OS never requires reading the manufacturer's image.

platforms.verdict: Hardware-wise the most open platform surveyed, and the only one where a full replacement OS is a coherent goal. Everything now rests on two cheap lid-off questions and one fuse.
openQuestions: Is the i.MX 6 serial-download path reachable, and are the HAB fuses unburned? Everything else is downstream of this.
Discrete PHY behind each etherCON, or straight to fabric?
Is anything in the clock tree steerable?
traps: A 3-byte magic such as gzip's appears about 2.3 times by chance in 38 MB, and scanning 514 transforms means scanning 263 MB — expect roughly 16 coincidental hits. An early verdict called the firmware "a known container" on exactly that basis.
Every negative sweep result needs a positive control. A broken sweep and a genuine absence look identical.

platforms.summary: Not a console, but the transport a great many of them hang off. Documented from both ends at once — the server firmware and the host driver are the same protocol version.
platforms.headline: The SoundGrid Server is a hard-realtime appliance, not a general-purpose Linux box. Its kernel command line isolates every worker core from the scheduler, RCU, tick, idle and frequency scaling, and SoundGrid frames are steered to a dedicated uncoalesced hardware receive queue.
platforms.method: Static analysis of vendor-distributed binaries and configuration files already present on a machine holding a licensed installation. No Waves source code, NDA material or SDK was involved. Techniques: reading plain-text scripts, demangling C++ symbol and RTTI tables, extracting strings, and disassembling a small number of functions in the GPL kernel module.

SGS firmware image `SGS_16.5`, External_Version 16.5.79.183 — extracted SquashFS
`AG_NSServer` — stripped ELF, retains C++ RTTI
`wsgnf.ko` — GPL-licensed kernel module, unstripped
141 × `.wfi` per-model I/O firmware files, referenced by name only

hardware.label: Boot

hardware.label: Base distribution

hardware.label: Kernel

hardware.label: Link layer
hardware.value: EtherType 0x8908, steered by ethtool receive-flow rules to hardware queue 1 with interrupt coalescing disabled (rx-frames 1, tx-frames 1)

software.label: Process model
software.value: A single userland process, `AG_NSServer` (AudioGrid Network Shell Server), owns the protocol. It starts before the network stack is brought up

software.label: Realtime partitioning
software.value: Command-line options name a control core, a master core and a worker core set, plus AudioGrid and kernel CPU reserve percentages

software.label: Kernel fast path

software.label: Protocol shape
software.value: Not a flat command set. A set of node families, each with its own protocol version, addressed by node number, each exposing a description-get operation plus family-specific commands

software.label: Self-description
software.value: The server can emit its own protocol description as XML (`-M`, node protocol xml). Capturing that output is the single highest-value next step

security.label: Scope boundary

security.label: GPL obligation

programmable.note: The stated goal: a device that appears on a SoundGrid network as a discoverable node, recovers the network sample clock, and exchanges multichannel audio with servers and I/O devices.

platforms.verdict: The most conventionally documentable platform here, because both sides of the same protocol version were available and corroborate each other — the driver names its C++ classes and the server names its message types.
openQuestions: No claim has been validated against live hardware. Nothing has been tested against a real SoundGrid network.
Every wire layout should be treated as provisional until a packet capture confirms it.
The XML self-description has not yet been captured from a running server.
traps: This is not black-box analysis and should never be described as such — the findings come substantially from inspecting vendor binaries.
It is not clean-room analysis either, because no implementation exists yet and therefore no team separation has been established. Both terms are commonly misapplied to work of this kind.

platforms.summary: A headless FPGA console whose mixing DSP is reconfigurable programmable-logic fabric loaded at every boot, running a full Ubuntu userland on a Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC — and whose update package quietly reveals the OEM behind the brand.
platforms.headline: The v1.2.3 update is a self-decrypting installer that unpacks to ten arm64 Debian packages. Their maintainer fields name the real makers — DSPRO Audio of Brazil for the platform, and audio developer George Yohng for the mixer core — while the payload ships the two Vivado bitstreams (`mixer128_main.bit`, `mixer128_aux.bit`) that ARE the mixing engine, loaded onto the PL through the Linux fpga_manager.
platforms.method: Static analysis of the single `dmix128_1.2.3.7045c05.dmixfw` update package: parsing the installer ELF, decrypting and unpacking its payload, and reading the resulting package control metadata, hardware-driver Python, FPGA register-map JSON and boot artifacts. No console was involved and no hardware was inspected.
artifacts: `dmix128_1.2.3.7045c05.dmixfw` — 70 MB update package (a stripped aarch64 ELF installer stub with an encrypted payload appended)

Ten `arm64` `.deb` packages: `dsmix`, `fxserver-zynq`, `mixer-web`, `mixer-extcontrol`, `mixer-local-gui`, `mixer-upgradedaemon-ng`, `nmos-bridge`, `button-monitor`, `xilinx-prog-zynqmp`, plus stock `avahi-utils`
`mixer128_main.bit` / `mixer128_aux.bit` — Vivado FPGA bitstreams; `dsmix_zu3.bin` / `dsmix_zu5.bin` — ZynqMP boot images
`Driver/Profiles/mixer128` and `mixer64` — JSON DSP register/routing maps; `Driver/misc/*.py` — hardware drivers

hardware.label: SoC
hardware.value: Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC (quad Cortex-A53 + programmable logic). The installer branches on a device-tree `device_id` of `zu3eg` or `zu5eg`

hardware.label: Model / SoC pairing
hardware.value: ZU3EG and ZU5EG boot images ship side by side (`dsmix_zu3.bin` / `dsmix_zu5.bin`); read as the smaller ZU3EG serving dMix 64 and the larger ZU5EG serving dMix 128

hardware.label: Mixing DSP
hardware.value: Reconfigurable FPGA fabric — two `.bit` bitstreams (`main` + `aux`) programmed onto the PL at boot via the mainline `fpga_manager` (`/sys/class/fpga_manager/fpga0/state`). No fixed-function mixing silicon

hardware.label: Clocking
hardware.value: Renesas VersaClock 6E generator, OTP-programmed over I²C by an in-tree driver

hardware.label: Board support
hardware.value: ADS1x15 ADC, PCA9536 GPIO expander, FTDI link and SPI NOR flash, driven from Python; hardware revision read from ZynqMP GPIO

hardware.label: Audio I/O
hardware.value: 96 kHz throughout; 32 head-amps, 32 AD / 28 DA, 2 AES3, 64 MADI, and 384 network (Dante/AES67) channels in the fabric map

software.label: Operating system
software.value: Ubuntu 24.04 aarch64 userland under systemd (packages built with GCC 13.3, Ubuntu 24.04)

software.label: Makers behind the brand
software.value: Package maintainers are DSPRO Audio (`dspro.com.br`) for the platform integration and George Yohng (`yohng.com`) for the mixer core — `Violet Audio` is the brand

software.label: Mixer application
software.value: `dsmix` is mypyc-compiled Python: a `Driver/` hardware-abstraction layer plus JSON register/routing maps for both `mixer128` and `mixer64` profiles. `fxserver-zynq` is the FX/DSP server against the fabric

software.label: Control plane
software.value: `mixer-extcontrol` (Go) serves the external protocols — ECP (Q-SYS), QRC, the zero-based VSKP keyspace and OSC — and additionally embeds an MCP/LLM "assistant" with an instrument-EQ preset knowledge base

software.label: Media control
software.value: `nmos-bridge` re-exposes the console as AMWA NMOS IS-04/05/08 senders and receivers (Python, Nuitka-compiled standalone)

software.label: Update mechanism
software.value: A Go `upgradedaemon` performs btrfs-snapshot A/B "checkpoint" upgrades — installing the packages, updating kernel and boot artifacts, and able to roll back to the previous snapshot

security.label: Update confidentiality / integrity
security.value: The `.dmixfw` payload is AES-256-CBC encrypted with a SHA-256 integrity check; the installer stub links OpenSSL and decrypts the payload to a temporary archive before unpacking

security.label: Update authenticity
security.value: Each package and the outer payload carry a 256-byte RSA-2048 signature; the `upgradedaemon` embeds an RSA-2048 public key and the signature-verification path is present in the binary

security.label: Recovery
security.value: The btrfs A/B checkpoint model provides rollback to the prior known-good snapshot if an upgrade is rejected or fails

programmable.item: The mixing engine is an FPGA bitstream
programmable.note: `mixer128_main.bit` and `mixer128_aux.bit` are loaded onto the PL at boot; the audio path is defined by programmable logic and the JSON register maps in `dsmix`, not by fixed silicon — the direct contrast to the Yamaha QL entry.
Dot-delimited keys such as `i.0.eq.b1.freq`, with `*` matching one component and `**` many. The same daemon also exposes ECP (Q-SYS), QRC and OSC.
`mixer-extcontrol` ships an agent that drives the console over MCP tools using an instrument-EQ knowledge base — an LLM-facing control surface baked into the firmware.

platforms.verdict: The most conventional computer in the index: a signed-and-encrypted Ubuntu appliance on a Zynq UltraScale+, where the mixing "hardware" is a bitstream shipped inside the same update as the web GUI. The teardown's real payoff is naming the OEM the brand doesn't — DSPRO Audio and George Yohng.
openQuestions: Whether the ZU3EG/ZU5EG split maps exactly to dMix 64 / dMix 128, and what the `main` vs `aux` bitstream division corresponds to in the signal path.
How much of the mixing math lives in the PL fabric versus the `fxserver-zynq` process, since the DSP register maps are declarative JSON.
Nothing here was checked against a running console; all findings are from the update package alone.
traps: The `.dmixfw` is not an archive — it is an executable installer with an encrypted payload appended after the ELF section headers, so ordinary archive tools see only a stripped binary.
The mixing DSP has no persistent firmware image on a flash chip to dump: it is a bitstream re-loaded into volatile fabric at every boot.

platforms.summary: Not a teardown. The open console these teardowns keep pointing at — included because "what would you build instead" is the question every one of them ends on.
platforms.headline: 128 inputs, 64 buses, every channel strip computed in FPGA fabric at 96 kHz, speaking Dante, RAVENNA/AES67 and AVB/Milan simultaneously. Where the commercial platforms hide the mixer behind an undocumented register map, here the register map is the deliverable.
platforms.method: Original design work. Correctness rests on a bit-accurate fixed-point model in Rust, replayed against the RTL in Verilator.
artifacts: Engineering specification — numbered, verifiable requirements
Fixed-point model and Verilator testbenches
